conventions.convention: Spacetime is an affine space A over a four-dimensional real vector space V, with surjective absolute-time map τ:V→R, spatial displacement space K=ker τ, positive-definite inner product g on K, and fixed orientation. Spatial distances apply only within simultaneous slices.

An inertial frame is an adapted affine chart (o,u,(e₁,e₂,e₃)), with τ(u)=1 and a fixed positively oriented g-orthonormal spatial basis. Frame changes use t′=t+b and x′=Rx+vt+a, with R∈SO(3); the boost sign is positive.

There are N≥1 particle labels with fixed positive masses. A particle worldline is C² on a nondegenerate open interval I and satisfies τ(γ(s)−o)=s. A time shift b changes its description to γ_b(t′)=γ(t′−b) on I+b.

Dimensions form the free abelian group generated by length ℓ, duration τ and mass μ. Coordinates use metres and seconds, masses kilograms, and rotation entries and radian angles are dimensionless. Numerical coordinates acquire physical dimensions through their unit declarations.

The unconstrained configuration domain is a stated open subset of R^(3N). The holonomic branch requires smooth G:O→R^k, 1≤k≤3N−1, nonempty G⁻¹(0), and rank DG=k throughout that fibre. The mass operator acts blockwise by the fixed masses.

Coordinate velocity and acceleration are x′ and x″. Spatial velocity is γ′−u and depends on the frame time direction; spatial acceleration is γ″∈K and is unchanged at corresponding events by an inertial frame change, although its coordinate triple rotates.

load_bearing.statement: Adopt spacetime data consisting of a four-dimensional real vector space V, a surjective linear absolute-time map τ, an inner product and orientation on K=ker τ, and an affine event space A modelled on V, with the affine smooth structure.

An inertial frame is the global adapted affine chart determined by o∈A, u∈V with τ(u)=1, and an ordered, g-orthonormal, positively oriented basis of K. Allowed changes between frames are t′=t+b, x′=Rx+vt+a, with R∈SO(3).

Particle labels i=1,…,N, N≥1, have C² worldlines γ_i:I→A on nondegenerate open intervals satisfying τ(γ_i(t)−o)=t, with frame descriptions related by the stated time shifts; each label carries a fixed positive mass, constant in time and across inertial frames.

A dimension is a triple (a,b,c)∈Z³ written ℓ^aτ^bμ^c; products and inverses use componentwise addition and negation. Products, quotients and derivatives obey the stated dimension rules, and quantities use the corresponding metre-second-kilogram reference units.

For two inertial frames and a worldline γ:I→A described in the first, η(t′)=x′(γ(t′−b)) on I+b is C² and satisfies η′(t′)=Rw(t′−b)+v and η″(t′)=Ra(t′−b). Acceleration vanishes identically in one frame iff it does in the other. The displayed composition and inverse laws make the Galilean transformations a group.

The unconstrained branch takes an open Q⊆R^(3N). The constrained branch takes Q=G⁻¹(0) for smooth G:O→R^k with nonempty zero set and surjective DG on it, giving an embedded configuration manifold of dimension 3N−k. The mass operator is M(x₁,…,x_N)=(m₁x₁,…,m_Nx_N).

The regular-value condition in the configuration definition, including the distinction between regularity and nonempty fibre.
The embedded-submanifold conclusion and inherited topology of constrained configuration spaces.
Dimension 3N−k under smoothness, regular-value and nonempty-fibre hypotheses; in particular the five-dimensional rigid-rod configuration space.
Differentiating time-shifted coordinate curves and sine/cosine compositions with the linear angular argument.
Norm and inner-product conventions, positive definiteness, and the squared-distance rigid-rod calculation.
The trigonometric functions appearing in the rotating-basis example.
Derivative identities and values at zero in the rotating-basis computation.
Orthonormality and orientation of the rotating basis, and nonvanishing of its coordinate curve.

concerns.concern: Clause (d) says: 'On the constrained branch the mass metric restricts the Euclidean inner product to Q as in that item.' The cited def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric instead defines G_q(u,v)=⟨dX_q(u),M dX_q(v)⟩. This is the restriction of the mass-weighted ambient form to tangent spaces, not generally the Euclidean inner product itself. The cited formula resolves the intended construction, but this sentence should agree with it.

Statement clause 3 additionally identifies zero acceleration with the coordinate curve being affine in frame time. Proof step 4.1 establishes frame-independence of zero acceleration but does not explicitly establish that additional equivalence. Componentwise application of the zero-derivative theorem on the interval, first to x′ and then to x minus its affine candidate, closes this immediately.

The Example introduces 'Let ω>0' and immediately uses sin(ωs) and cos(ωs), with s read in seconds, without declaring ω's dimension and reference unit locally. The sibling dimension-bookkeeping example subsequently declares [ω]=τ⁻¹, but this example should itself state inverse-time units so its trigonometric arguments are explicitly dimensionless.

alerts.finding: The associated page cm15-scattering-and-impulse-model-boundaries-examples summarizes this item as 'the elastic case exchanges the velocities'. For its declared unequal masses m₁=2, m₂=6 kg and incoming velocities 3 and −1 m/s, the item correctly states and computes outgoing velocities −3 and +1 m/s in Verification 2.1. These are reversals, not an exchange of the incoming velocities. The discrepancy is in the B-page summary; the item's computation is sound.

The final paragraph says 'The Galilean transformations are exact symmetries of the adopted model by [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]]'. That supplier proves the kinematic frame-change laws and group structure; it does not establish dynamical symmetry of every declared force model. post-cm01-frames clause (vi) explicitly warns that conservation and invariance of a mechanical system's description need additional force-law hypotheses. The sentence should specify the kinematic structure or distinguish passive covariance from a symmetry of a fixed interaction model.
